title: Workflow Basics and Tools: Non-layer Post-Processing for Landscape Imagery in Photoshop

date.basis: Embedded file creation_time metadata indicates 2024-10-17T11:57:41Z; transcript reinforces techniques typical of contemporary Photoshop versions.

locations.name: Himalayas or Karakoram region (probable)
locations.basis: Transcript explicitly references the Himalayas or Karakoram as the source location for the image.

summary: The presenter walks through a landscape-post workflow in Photoshop that minimizes layering in favor of a fast, paint-on-canvas approach. Starting from a pre-processed image, they emphasize Camera Raw Filter as a primary access point to raw-style adjustments without returning to Lightroom, advocate for a limited toolset for speed, and demonstrate selective color, color grading, and masking to shape tonal values and atmosphere. The talk covers practical tricks for focus stacking with Photoshop’s Load Files Into Stack, selective color masking for targeted color edits, and the use of warps to alter form—with cautions about distortion. The session also includes workflow organization: using history states, the history brush, and versioning saves to preserve different iterations. Overall, the video serves as a compact, repeatable toolkit (roughly 10–12 core tools) presented as a fast, hands-on system rather than a comprehensive tutorial on every available Photoshop feature.

sections.title: Intro and no-layer workflow philosophy
concepts: Starting from an already processed image
Preference for a layer-minimal, painterly approach
Camera Raw Filter as a quick entry point; avoidance of Lightroom for speed
Only rare use of layers (e.g., focus stacking)
sections.description: The presenter explains a fast, layer-light workflow in Photoshop, using a Himalayas/Karakoram-origin image as the example. They propose editing with a paint-on-canvas mindset, preferring to apply adjustments directly rather than on many separate layers and explaining how Camera Raw Filter provides raw-tools access without leaving Photoshop.

sections.title: Raw processing, Camera Raw integration, and dynamic range controls
concepts: Returning to raw adjustments via Camera Raw Filter
Why Lightroom is not used here
Dynamic range concepts: shadows, whites, blacks; avoiding heavy overall contrast
Exposure vs. tonal adjustments; 3-stop shadow recovery caveats for certain gear
sections.description: The speaker demonstrates invoking Camera Raw Filter from within Photoshop to adjust the image as if editing a raw file, highlighting the speed advantage and noting that Lightroom is slower for this workflow. They discuss the dynamic range panel (the light panel) for shadows and highlights, emphasizing shadows/whites/blacks over contrast in typical landscape edits, and explain constraints related to equipment.

sections.title: Color grading, masking, and selective color fundamentals
concepts: Color temperature and tint as primary color controls
Selective Color as a foundational tool; masking capabilities
Color grading as a tonal-color coupling tool
Preserving luminosity while adjusting color palettes
sections.description: This section delves into color control hierarchy, stressing temperature/tint for base color balance, and elevates selective color as a powerful yet complex masking-aware tool. The presenter demonstrates how to target specific colors and tonal regions to adjust mood without introducing global artifacts.

sections.title: Selective color masking and deep-dive into color tools
concepts: Masking with selective color to affect blacks, whites, shadows, and highlights
Relative vs absolute color adjustments to control banding
Preserving luminosity and maintaining color relationships
sections.description: The video emphasizes using selective color as a masking tool to selectively colorize or desaturate particular tonal ranges. Relative adjustments help avoid hard banding, and masking is highlighted as a key capability to constrain edits to specific areas like the sky or foliage.

sections.title: Layers, history-based editing, and non-destructive iteration
concepts: Introduction to history states (default 1000) for non-destructive editing
History brush as a primary painting tool to apply prior adjustments
Check-marked steps and selective application across the image
Versions and saving: creating parallel files for comparison
sections.description: The presenter outlines a history-driven workflow: enabling many history states, using the history brush to apply past edits selectively, and saving multiple versions to compare progress later. This section also covers how to safely apply or erase adjustments while preserving the ability to revert.

sections.title: Focus stacking and array of practical filters
concepts: Load files into stack to enable focus stacking
Helicon Focus as a potential alternative
Alignment and auto-blend steps; transparent fill for non-overlapping areas
sections.description: Discussion centers on constructing focus stacks in Photoshop, with mention of external tools like Helicon Focus as a possible alternative. The workflow includes saving, auto-aligning, and auto-blending while ensuring transparency fill to handle blank regions.

System setup: increasing history states for non-destructive exploration
Wrap-up and a hint at more to come
sections.description: The speaker recaps the essential toolkit (about 10–12 tools) and emphasizes configuring Photoshop for high history-state capacity. The closing notes preview further training and tomorrow’s continuation.
